globalRules: Always reference a specific detail from the contact's notes so the message feels personal, not templated.
Keep first-touch messages short — three sentences or fewer.
Every message needs a clear primary ask (try it or buy it), and a referral ask only where it fits naturally.

When offering to 'send' or 'give' a product, make the exact nature of the offer explicit (e.g. free sample/referral opportunity, friends and family discount, or purchase link) — don't leave it ambiguous whether it's a gift or a sale.

Don't blend gift language ('send you', 'give you') with discount/pricing language ('my family discount') in the same offer — pick one framing explicitly: either 'this one's on me, no charge' (free gift) or 'here's my friends & family discount link' (paid, discounted). Mixing both leaves the recipient unsure if they'll be charged.

close: For close contacts, lead with the relationship — ask about their life before mentioning Ember & Oak.

When a close contact is going through a major life event (wedding, baby, big milestone), explicitly ask them to refer people in their event's orbit (bridesmaids, guests, etc.) with a friends & family discount link — these moments are natural referral goldmines.
warm: For warm contacts, reference the specific shared context (how you know them) before mentioning the product.
acquaintance: Keep acquaintance messages low-pressure and easy to ignore — no hard call-to-action, no urgency language.

timing: Wait at least 3 days after a reply before sending a follow-up.
askStyle: Default to a direct ask (try it / buy it) unless the contact's notes suggest they're not a personal fit — then lead with a referral ask instead.

When the referral ask is the lead (because the contact isn't a personal fit), make it a direct, specific question — e.g. 'Do you know anyone who'd love this?' — rather than a passive, open-ended offer like 'if you ever cross paths with someone...' or 'let me know in the future,' which rarely prompts action.
